messages.body_plain:
Probably this means that the result of BAYAREALIKE is producing e=5, and when that is put into BAYAREALIKE+J as the init (initial) value, that means it's outside your min and max since the default max is 4.99999 or whatever.

It's very odd to get a parameter hitting the maximum limit, this means you have optimization problems (you have not actually found the maximum of the likelihood, instead, you hit the parameter max before you got there).

Options:

1. Change the max

2. Double-check your tree. New users sometimes put in inappropriate trees, often undated trees where the branchlengths are not in millions of years. Short branches lead to high parameter values, amongst other problems:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#fix_short_trees

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: Fix to set.seed over-run problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Fix to a bug, already uploaded to PhyloWiki:

On Mon, Jun 6, 2016 at 7:50 PM, XXX wrote:
> Hey Nick,
>
> I can report that fixing the stratification files also fixed the problem.
>
> I realized, though, that this was one of two errors I was getting leading to unsuccessful mapping. The other one is:
>
> Error in set.seed(seed = seedval) : supplied seed is not a valid integer
> In addition: Warning message:
> In set.seed(seed = seedval) : NAs introduced by coercion to integer range
>
> I’ve tried changing the seed value or removing it altogether, and I still get the message, but strangely only with certain trees (attached is a reproducible example with XXX and associated files).
>
> Thanks (again!) for all your help with this,
>

Hi -- oh, this was an integer over-run, this never occurred on my small test examples.  To force the seed to be (a) changing every step but (b) deterministic based on the starting seed, I had a function calculating it by adding treepiece_seed_counter * treepiece_seed_counter_increment, and this was added incrementally through the list of tree pieces in a stratified analysis. This leads to the over-run on large problems I guess.

You can see the error here:
set.seed(2147483647)
set.seed(2147483648)

I'm adding a check that will use the remainder of (seed/2147483647) if the seed is over 2147483647...it looks like your file is working now, so I've uploaded it (and added the check several other places also).

Cheers, thanks for the bug report as always, you are giving the software a workout!

Cheers, Nick

messages.subject: Solution to "object 'brlen_in_section' not found"
messages.body_plain:
This error was reported awhile back, but not reproducibly.  It turns out it was due to

(a) time-stratified analysis where
(b) the oldest time in the times file was not older than the root of the tree

I've now added a check to the check_BioGeoBEARS_run function to check for this.  However, sometimes people forget to look at the output of check_BioGeoBEARS_run(), so I'm putting the error message and solution here also.

Cheers!
Nick

On Sun, Jun 5, 2016 at 9:58 PM, XXX wrote:
> Hey Nick,
>
> Thanks so much for the quick turnaround on that bug report--it got things up and working.
>
> Sorry to hit you up for something else right away, but for about 10% of the fits for which I've been building stochastic maps, I'm unable to successfully create any maps.The error I get is:
>
> Error in stochastic_map_branch(nodenum_at_top_of_branch = right_branch_decnode,  :
>   object 'brlen_in_section' not found
>
> I noticed that this has already come up on the google group (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/biogeobears/LrmQGQ6bZ94/BPc_0QsQCQAJ), but I'm wondering if you have any other tips for what I should try to change going forward.
>
> I've attached a .zip file including XXX and the associated files needed to reproduce the error. Thanks in advance!!
>
> I noticed you'll be at Evolution--I look forward to seeing you there!
>
> Best,
>
> XXX

Hi -- this could be due to your times file, which only goes down to 60 Ma even though the bottom of your tree is ~72 Ma.  Add a new time bin that goes to e.g. 75 Ma (below the bottom of the tree), and make the other matrices match (copy the last matrix, or whatever you think is appropriate), and re-run...see if that fixes it.

Cheers!
Nick

Re: your question, dstart etc are just ways to use the d estimate from eg DEC for the starting point of eg DEC+J. This can help you check ML optimization - please read PhyloWiki for advice on double-checking ML optimization. But it's not required.

For w, the fixed default is w=1 so run a model with w fixed to 1 (eg regular DEC+J) and another with w free, eg DEC+J+w.

Note for everyone : understanding the concepts of nested models and the concept that adding a free parameter should always equal or improve the likelihood (if it doesn't then you have optimization problems) is really a key requirement for doing model comparison in BGB or any other software. I have put a lot of tips on the phylowiki since I see these basics misunderstood a lot, sometimes even by reviewers...  Cheers! Nick

SYMPOSIUM INFORMATION

Symposium: SSB1
Title: Putting evolution into ecological niche modeling: Building the connection between phylogenies, paleobiology, and species distribution models
Co-organizers: Nicholas J. Matzke and Dan Warren

Summary

(link to this section)

Summary: Species Distribution Models (SDMs) are increasingly popular tools in ecology, conservation biology, and climate change research. They have been used in hundreds of publications (Figure 1). The most common SDM methods correlate occurrence data with environmental variables, estimating an ecological or environmental niche model (ENM). This niche model is then projected onto a map to predict species distribution (or suitable habitat). Despite their immense popularity, SDM results are often limited by several common problems. Large data sets allow complex correlational models to be fit, but these models are often over-fit, extrapolating poorly to changed environments in the past 1,2 (when predicting paleo-distributions) or present 3 (when predicting species invasions). This lowers confidence in SDMs predicted under future climate change scenarios. Also, SDMs typically assume that geographic range is wholly determined by environment, ignoring dispersal limitation and other historical biogeography processes 4,5, as well as species interactions. This means that ENMs may include some environmental variables as predictors when they are only "accidental" correlates of some other spatial process, further contributing to the overfitting problem.

The fundamental issue underlying the above difficulties is that the SDMs are typically estimated one-species-at-a-time, at one time point (the Recent). This ignores any information that might be gained from the phylogenetic relationships of species, even though phylogenetic niche conservatism appears to be common 4. It also ignores any information that might be gained from time-series data on distributions and climate. As evolutionary biologists, we should be seeking ways to make evolutionary methods and models useful to the wider scientific community, and it seems likely that by combining information on present-day niches distributions, and how niches and distributions evolved on the phylogeny, will provide both evolutionary insight and improved niche models that more robust and do better at capturing the true predictors of species ranges 4. Therefore Symposium will be devoted to "building the connection" between SDMs and phylogenies. How can we integrate phylogenetic models of niche evolution and trait evolution into the SDM estimation process? How can we better integrate paleoclimate and paleo-range data, and historical biogeography? The Symposium will solicit contributions from researchers at the forefront of relevant areas, whether or not they consider themselves "species distribution modelers" per se. For example, workers in phylogenetic comparative methods and evolutionary morphometrics will have much to contribute to the question of how niche evolution should be modeled and estimated, as do conservation biologists who take into phylogenetic relatedness and diversity 6,7, and paleobiologists who have examined the congruence of SDM predictions and fossil occurrences 1,2,8-11. All symposium speakers will be asked to connect their research to the overall question, "How can we connect phylogeny, paleobiology, and species distribution modeling?"
